newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bankruptcy debt up nearly 40% in Dec yr/yr.
newsitem.headline: Japan bankruptcy debt up nearly 40% in Dec yr/yr.

text.p: Total debt held by bankrupt firms in Japan in December rose nearly 40 percent from a year ago to 598.1 billion yen, a private research and rating company said on Tuesday.
Prolonged sluggishness in the economy continued to be the main cause for the failures, Tokyo Commerce and Industry Research Co said in a regular report on bankruptcies.
"The number of bankruptcies induced by the economic slump continues to be at an alarming level, especially among small and medium-sized firms," Tokyo Commerce said.
The number of large-scale failures involving debts of more than one billion yen declined in December to 67 cases from November's 75, but was still up from October's 48.
The major failures in December included Apollo Finance, which applied to the Tokyo District Court for corporate restructuring under Japan's bankruptcy laws with debts totalling about 111 billion yen.
The company is part of the same group as the insolvent Cosmo Credit Union.
The number of companies filing for bankruptcy in Japan in December declined 1.1 percent from a year ago to 1,279.
Bankruptcies caused by weak economic conditions accounted for 58.8 percent of the total, the report said.
A total of 587 failures were due to sluggish sales, while 136 were caused by accumulated losses and 30 by trouble collecting money owed, the report said.
"The economic outlook is dim," the report said.

It said that there is a widening gap between the earnings of companies that are doing well and those that are not doing well within the same industry, due to such reasons as changing consumption patterns.
Tokyo Commerce also said in a separate report on Tuesday that total bankruptcy debts in 1996 declined 12.1 percent from the previous year to 8.12 trillion yen.
However, the annual figure was still the third largest ever, the report said. Total debt hit a record high of 9.24 trillion yen last year.
The number of large-scale bankruptcies involving debts of more than 100 billion totalled nine.
Such cases included non-bank Nichiei Finance Co Ltd with total debts of more than one trillion yen, the largest insolvency case in Japan in the post-war period.
There was also the failure of major realtor Sueno Kosan, which collapsed with debts of about 716 billion yen. Sueno borrowed heavily from failed "jusen" mortgage firms.
The number of failures in 1996 slightly decreased by 1.8 percent from 1995 to 1,434, the report said.
A major portion of the failures were among small and medium-sized companies which could not adjust to the changing economic structure, the report said.

Failures caused by weak economic conditions accounted for 59.7 percent of the total in 1996. It was the fourth consecutive year that such failures accounted for more than half of the annual total, the report said.

"While big companies successfully restructured themselves via cost-cutting by shifting some operations overseas and reducing employees, many domestic demand-driven firms have not been profitable because of high production costs and falling prices," said the report.
Tokyo Commerce also said it expects the number of bankrupties in 1997 to total more than 15,000, slightly more than last year's 14,834.
